implementation_notes: Interlocked is the .NET atomic surface: CompareExchange, Exchange, Increment/Decrement, Add, and the newer generic Interlocked.CompareExchange<T>. System.Threading.Volatile provides the memory barriers for ordinary reads and writes (Volatile.Read/Write), which is how you pair a plain field with a release publication. Volatile.Read/Write by itself is only a barrier, not a compare-and-swap, so it is not enough for a lock-free structure - that distinction is the source of most .NET concurrency bugs. Interlocked operations are full fences, which is correct but heavier than the acquire/release pair the pattern wants, so prefer Volatile plus Interlocked.CompareExchange for the publish pattern.
idiom_name: System.Threading.Interlocked for the RMW; Volatile.Read/Write for the acquire/release pair
pitfalls: Volatile.Read/Write are barriers, not atomic read-modify-write: Volatile.Write(x, x+1) is a read-modify-write race, and this is the most common .NET concurrency bug.
Interlocked operations are full barriers, so using Interlocked for the acquire/release publish is correct but pays for more than the pattern needs.
Volatile.Read of a generic T boxes unless T is a reference or a primitive; use Interlocked.Read for 64-bit values on 32-bit targets.
Interlocked.CompareExchange on a non-atomic field does not make the surrounding plain accesses ordered - the whole protocol must participate.
